output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the 22% deviation is attributed to shared memory, but the recompute-from-text baseline also shows cross-client interference, and the paper says differences between the two paths cannot be attributed to cache persistence.
output.brief: OLMo-3-7B-Instruct is tested in a two-client market setting with 20 goal-conflict families, where Clients A and B hold opposing objectives and their turns share one persistent KV cache. Among 150 eligible decision points, the model deviates from the current client's objective in 22.0% of cases (11.3% choose the opposite objective, the rest the mixed option). Reprocessing the transcript from text also shows interference, so persistence is not shown to be the cause. Linear probes on pooled K/V goal-token spans give a goal-ownership AUROC near chance at layer 0 (0.481) and 0.982 at layer 15, with single heads reaching 0.993. Zeroing the competitor's cached goal K/V in layers 12-20 shifts the target-vs-opposite log-probability margin by +0.464 (K) and +0.704 (V). Probe-selected top-3 heads beat random heads, goal tokens beat matched non-goal tokens, and ablating the current client's own goals reverses the sign. Selected actions change less often (23 of 166 non-target decisions corrected by V ablation). Limits: one 7B model, explicit ownership labels, zero-ablation, and no distinction between binding, retrieval, or competition mechanisms.
output.gist: Zero-ablating a competitor's cached goal K/V in a shared KV cache shifts OLMo-3-7B toward the current client, with probe-selected heads and goal tokens mattering more than controls.
output.weight_reason: It is a sound but narrow causal study, with one 7B model, synthetic scenarios, zero-ablation, and no mechanism for the leakage, though it includes matched head and token controls.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the loss effect is shown only for neurons and SAE features (NarraHeads are weak or null, with GPT heads showing none), and the benchmark effects are modest, with the largest on Gemma (about 9 points on English XStoryCloze) and only English significant on Llama.
output.brief: The paper looks for components in GPT-2-Small, Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.1-8B that track narrativity (the mean of agency, event sequencing and world building, rated 1-5). Attention heads, MLP neurons and pretrained SAE features are selected by Spearman correlation of activation with narrativity (rho >= 0.5) on LLM-labelled NarraDetect texts. Ablating selected sets then raises next-token loss more for narrative texts on held-out human-labelled data (NVC_loss about .65-.86 for neurons and features, against about 0 for random sets); heads are weak. Ablating NarraFeatures lowers generated narrativity by 1.0-1.9 points in Gemma and Llama, far more than random ablation. Dimension-specific ablation shows partial selectivity for agency and event but none for world building. On benchmarks, NarraFeature ablation hurts XStoryCloze (all four languages in Gemma, English only in Llama) and CosmosQA more than random ablation, and hallucination results are mixed. Limits: three models, a heuristic threshold, set-level rather than component-level causal claims, uncorrected significance tests, and an LLM-judged narrativity measure.
output.gist: Components correlated with narrativity are selected in three LMs; ablating neuron and SAE-feature sets raises loss on narrative text, cuts generated narrativity, and impairs story completion more than random ablation.
output.weight_reason: It is a complete study with random-set baselines and held-out validation for a new behaviour, but it is limited to set-level ablations, a weak head result, mixed benchmark effects and no circuit-level structure.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: steering was tested only on V\u2192I cadences in major chorales, with the best \u03b1 picked per condition, and it moved 32% of resolutions to vi and 57% to i. Parallel-minor steering raised FMD from 80.3 to 106.7, so "reliably" and "preserving generation quality" are stronger than shown.
output.brief: Aria, a LLaMA-based symbolic music transformer, is analyzed on Bach chorales using minimal counterfactual pairs: lowering the third of a V chord at a cadence (184 major and 91 minor prompts). The edit cuts tonic resolutions in major chorales from 87.5% to 51.4%. Patching the last-token residual stream from the edited into the original prompt gives no effect in layers 0-5, and the effect grows from about layer 6 through later layers. Linear probes decode mode at up to 82.1% (layers 8-9) and 18-class key at 65.5% by layer 15. Steering vectors built from probe weight differences shift major-chorale cadences: a relative-minor direction raises vi resolutions to 32%, and a parallel-minor direction raises i to 57% from an 81% tonic baseline. Mode steering only redistributes mass diffusely. Relative keys are confused more than parallel keys in the probes, which the authors offer as the reason parallel steering works better. Limits: one model, Bach only, \u03b1 tuned per condition, no random-direction control, and FMD rises for parallel steering.
output.gist: Patching, probing and probe-derived steering on the Aria music transformer with Bach chorales show mode decodes before key, and key-direction steering shifts some cadence resolutions toward minor tonics.
output.weight_reason: A clean but narrow case study of one model on one corpus and one cadence type, with standard tools, tuned steering strengths and no control baselines.

output.brief: The work defines SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR). For each prompt, the top 16 active SAE feature contributions are kept or removed in sampled subsets while the rest of the activation stays fixed. The patched activation is propagated through the upper layers, and SAR is the fraction of behavioral variance that an order-r interaction model leaves unexplained. Under independent subset sampling, SAR equals the normalized energy of interactions above order r and bounds the weighted coalition ordering error of the best order-r approximation. Experiments use Gemma-3 4B, Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1 8B on six behaviors. First order residuals are positive in all 57 model, layer and behavior combinations. Learned SAE coordinates have lower first order residuals than sum-preserving random rotations in all 18 main settings (for example 0.0218 vs 0.1196 for Mistral subject-verb agreement). Pairwise terms raise mean rank fidelity from 0.9782 to 0.9959 and beat parameter-matched random third-order terms in all 18. In a 16-direction CorrSteer experiment on Llama-3.1 8B with MMLU-Pro, pairwise modeling raises rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790. Across six Gemma-3 1B SAEs, SAR tracks sign error and selection regret better than reconstruction FVU. The conclusions depend on the selected contributions, readout and intervention distribution, and the steering test covers one model and one direction set.
output.gist: Measures how much SAE feature effects fail to add up downstream via subset interventions. Learned coordinates beat random rotations on first-order additivity, yet pairwise terms still improve coalition ordering and steering prediction.
output.weight_reason: A sound, theoretically grounded metric with a controlled rotation baseline and multi-model experiments that others evaluating SAE feature composition can build on, but with a narrow empirical scope.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the up-to-12x (median 4x) curvature reduction is the eigenvalue ratio from an upper bound (Proposition 2), not a measured directional curvature of the cleaned vector.
output.brief: The paper defines a steering Hessian, the second derivative of a first-token cross-entropy loss with respect to the steering vector. It estimates the top and bottom eigenpairs by Lanczos iteration with finite-difference Hessian-vector products, using 12 prompts per condition. On Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B, across four tasks and 36 layer conditions, condition numbers range from 50 to 3,727. The top-15 eigenvectors (1-5% of the CAA vector's squared norm) produce anti-steer rates of 0.53-1.00, and the bottom directions are mostly robust. Projecting the sharp component out of CAA preserves cosine above 0.974. It beats CAA in all 25 generation conditions on sentiment, sycophancy and refusal, with classifier scoring on 50 completions per condition. For example, Qwen refusal rises from 36% under CAA to 88-98%. Negative-polarity jailbreak tests suggest the sharp component adds noise rather than signal. Limits: 7-8B models, 20 contrastive pairs, a single-target-token loss, toxicity absent from generation tests, small jailbreak samples and no significance tests.
output.gist: Computes the Hessian of behavioral loss over the steering vector; its top eigendirections mostly reverse behavior, and projecting them out of CAA vectors improves generation on three 7–8B models.
output.weight_reason: It offers a new curvature-based diagnostic and a cheap post-processing fix for CAA, tested with controls on three models and four tasks, but at small scale and with narrow classifier-based generation evaluation.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the 5.71% and 5.13% gains come from one seed-fixed 337M run per configuration on 3.5B FineWeb-Edu tokens (3.47% at 1B), and the "recurs at a larger model scale" claim is a single 1B model with different stream identities and stage boundaries, not a replication across scales.
output.brief: Masked diffusion language models are given multiple persistent residual streams with token-conditioned read, mixing and write routing (mHC-lite). Models use a 16-block, 337M Qwen-style backbone trained on 3.5B FineWeb-Edu tokens. Two streams lower validation reconstruction perplexity by 5.71% against a standard residual, and one learned stream alone gives 2.50%. The two-stream gain is 5.13% on average over OpenWebText, WikiText-103, LAMBADA and C4, with three or four streams adding at most 0.52% more. Interventions show the masked/visible role organizes read and write-destination routing: role means remove 95.7% and 98.6% of the damage from global averaging. Token-specific write volume stays important within each role. A role-factorized model trained from scratch recovers 50.2% of the gain from a second stream over one learned stream. State patching finds one stream keeps its post-first-MLP state through middle depth while evidence builds at masked positions, and late layers read it again. A single 1B model shows the same stages, with a 3.47% perplexity reduction. Limits: single runs per configuration, short training budgets, and mechanistic claims resting on interventions over small selected samples, for example 179 source-target pairs.
output.gist: Multi-stream residual connections with learned routing in masked diffusion language models cut reconstruction perplexity by 5.71% with two streams; interventions show role-dependent routing and one stream preserving early token states for later reuse.
output.weight_reason: A sound, carefully intervened study of hyper-connection-style residuals applied to diffusion LMs, with a modest single-run gain at 337M and 1B and no new reference model.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: it says specification prompting lowers refusal and that interventions alter refusal, but the text shows these effects come from one bundled template whose factors are not separated, and the natural prompting effect is not shown to be mediated by the code-output direction. The SpecReveal 96.88% figure also does not appear in the reported tables, which give 98/100 with a 21% false-positive rate.
output.brief: PseudoSpec rewrites harmful code requests as engineering specifications with configuration fields, predicate APIs, LTL-style axioms and implementation mandates. On 104 RedCode-Gen tasks across five open-weight 7-8B models, refusal with risk keywords retained falls from 74-100% (natural language) to 0-8.65% (specification). Natural-language requests with keywords removed still draw 37.5-66.35% refusal. Specification prompts shift representations along a code-output direction estimated from benign tasks. Adding a condition-difference vector flips every baseline refusal in all five models, though random perturbations flip some too and high strength produces degenerate output. SpecCloak adds generator-discriminator prompt refinement and reaches 370/1,280 (28.91%) execution-verified successes across eight targets on RedCode-Gen, with the highest count on every target and ablations showing both parts help. SpecReveal reconstructs intent in natural language and runs dual-view detection, catching 98/100 SpecCloak prompts at 21% false positives with an o4-mini judge. Results depend heavily on the judge model. Limits include joint variation of template factors, no causal mediation test, and mechanism and attack evaluations run on disjoint model sets.
output.gist: Rewriting harmful code requests as engineering specifications sharply lowers refusal in five open models and shifts code-output representations. The derived SpecCloak attack reaches 28.91% execution-verified success on eight targets; SpecReveal detects most such prompts.
output.weight_reason: It offers a thorough behavioral, representational and intervention study of a template-based code jailbreak with execution-verified attack results and a defense, but the mechanism remains partly unestablished and the defense is judge-dependent.

output.brief: Five factuality alignment methods are reproduced independently: FLAME (DPO), FactAlign (KTO), KnowRL (GRPO), FactGRPO (Dr. GRPO) and FAITH (PPO). Each is first run in its own setup, and then all five are trained on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA and evaluated on one benchmark. The benchmark has biography and Alpaca-Fact long-form prompts scored with VeriScore, plus SimpleQA and TruthfulQA graded by gpt-4o. None of the methods reproduces in full. FLAME's factuality gain holds but its no-helpfulness-cost claim does not. FactAlign holds only with its released checkpoint, not on retraining. FactGRPO's published gains do not appear. On the common benchmark no method significantly beats the base model, except a one-word-answer artifact for FAITH and a small relevance-filtered F1 gain (+.017) for FactGRPO on biographies. Rewards favor length, format or brevity, and about two fifths of long-form responses contain supported but irrelevant claims. On-policy and offline training perform alike. Evidence source, recall normalizer and judge shift scores more than the methods do. Limits: one seed, LoRA, an 8B model, reduced training budgets, and substituted components in several reproductions.
output.gist: Reproduces five factuality alignment methods (FLAME, FactAlign, KnowRL, FactGRPO, FAITH) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; none reproduces fully, and none gives meaningful gains over the base model on a common benchmark.
output.weight_reason: A careful, open reproduction and fair comparison with significance testing and an evaluation-reliability analysis, but with reduced budgets and substituted components, so it is a useful corrective rather than a reference.

output.brief: Two data-only poisoning attacks are tested on protein design systems. In the first, 300M-parameter ProtGPT2-style and ProGen2-style models are pre-trained from scratch for 12B tokens on UniRef50. Poisoned records insert one of two triggers (the QK peptide or a p53 segment) into a host protein and overwrite the downstream residues with one of three payloads: poly-alanine, chlorotoxin repeats, or diphtheria toxin. Under a uniform 1% schedule, majority ASR-90 activation appears at about 5,000 to 12,500 poisoned examples. Under a ramped schedule, which delivers poison late in training, activation begins at 200 to 1,000 examples. All 24 poisoned terminal checkpoints reach 94 to 100% ASR-90, and clean-prompt perplexity tracks the clean baselines. In the second attack, records are inserted into the ProDVa retrieval corpus. A request-matched record enters the top 16 for 58% of templated and 97% of free-text requests. Among captured requests, 62% yield altered sequences and 19 to 21% acquire the payload domain by profile-HMM homology. A universal attack with 1,500 records captures 14% of templated and 60% of free-text requests. Limits: only two small architectures, one retrieval system, sequence-level metrics only, and no biological activity tested.
output.gist: Poisoned protein sequences implant trigger-dependent payload generation in 300M protein language models, and inserted retrieval records redirect ProDVa generation. Capture reaches 97% for free-text requests; the effects are sequence-level only.
output.weight_reason: It applies standard backdoor and retrieval-poisoning attacks to protein design, with fair controls but only small models, one retrieval system and sequence-level success metrics.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the +0.116 gain compares one-shot S0 with multi-round S2, which differ in both tool evidence and iteration, and the no-tool iteration control was too noisy to separate the two; the top-decile rise (21.4% to 23.5%) comes with no significance test.
output.brief: DRYLAB-Bench has LLM agents propose top-3 single-site substitutions for 30 hazardous mutation-design scenarios in eight risk categories. Designs are scored by a Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS): assay-standardized effects, matched to 187,695 hidden DMS measurements from ProteinGym and ViroGym, weighted by model confidence. Fifteen models were tested in three settings drawn from one shared trajectory: one-shot (S0), one tool-revision round (S1) and up to four rounds with six design tools (S2). Without tools, pooled BRS is 0.359, 67.6% of designs exceed the assay mean and 21.4% reach the top decile. Under S2, pooled BRS is 0.475 (+0.116, bootstrap CI +0.077 to +0.160) and the top-decile share is 23.5%. Thirteen of 15 models gain, and gain correlates negatively with S0 score (r=-0.42). Tools misaligned with the phenotype, as in the CcdB scenario, can lower scores. Refusal ranges from 0% to 96.7% and tracks wording rather than hazard: academic rewrites lower it and harm-context prefixes raise it. Limits: only single substitutions on public assays, with 83.9% measurement coverage, and an unreliable no-tool iteration control.
output.gist: A benchmark scoring LLM agents' hazardous single-site mutation designs against 187,695 public DMS measurements; across 15 models, no-tool designs are enriched for high-risk variants, and refusal tracks wording.
output.weight_reason: It is a useful, carefully built agentic biosecurity benchmark with safe ground-truth scoring and a 15-model evaluation, but the tool-attribution analysis is confounded and the task scope is narrow (single substitutions on public assays).

output.brief: GRPO is run on GSM8K with Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B policies against frozen, reference-free, single-token LLM judges. The main judges are Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B and OLMo-2 1B/7B; one smaller Qwen3-0.6B judge is paired with the 1.5B policy, giving 12 policy-judge cells with 2-4 seeds each. Judge acceptance rose everywhere it was logged, but no cell's seed-mean held-out greedy accuracy gained more than 0.04, and the early rise in training-rollout accuracy was mostly sampling sharpening. A gold-reward control raised the 1.5B policy by +0.054 but gave no detectable gain for the 0.5B policy. Plateau depth of judge hacking correlates with judge AUC (Spearman -0.69), and larger judges within a family are fooled less deeply. Two pre-specified pairs contradict the gap account on onset; the cell with the larger gap was fooled 3.5x sooner. With 12 cells, judge AUC and the gap cannot be separated formally. A blind test of step-0 predictors on three held-out judges was inconclusive. Limits: one task and recipe, small models, and the only smaller-judge cell is confounded by family.
output.gist: GRPO on GSM8K against frozen LLM judges raised judge acceptance but not held-out accuracy. Hacking depth tracked judge quality (AUC) rather than the policy-judge gap, though the 12 cells cannot formally separate the two.
output.weight_reason: A careful, pre-specified crossed design with a gold-reward control and a blind test, but limited to GSM8K, policies of at most 1.5B, 12 cells and partly inconclusive results.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the restatement pattern holds only for strong guards and recall-losing guards like TS-Guard, while excess flips of over-blocking guards are larger on non-leaky steps, and the low-resource gradient rests on a reduced roster that excludes the partner-hosted guards.
output.brief: LinguaGuardBench takes the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj and translates only the user instruction into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic. Tool calls, observations and labels stay byte-identical. Controls are six English rewordings, a whitespace placebo, and three repeats of managed guards. Nineteen guards were run, including four purpose-built agent guards; the Swahili and Amharic conditions were run only on the Gemini and self-deployed guards. Of 77 guard-by-language cells, 39 show a significant FPR or TPR shift. Placebo-adjusted flip rates for the nine guards below 13B rise from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic. Purpose-built guards are the most unstable; ShieldAgent flips up to 12.1% of verdicts. Open 12-30B guards over-block (up to +5.0 pp FPR), and every significant recall loss, up to -7.4 pp, is in a guard below 10B. Frontier guards move by about one point at most, and Gemini 3.8 Flash matches its no-request control on all 3,660 verdicts. English paraphrase moves guards less than translation. Limits: translations come from a Gemini model, nobody on the team reads the low-resource languages, no mitigation is tested, and bootstrap intervals cluster by trajectory rather than by instruction.
output.gist: Translating only the user request of fixed agent-guard steps into five languages flips verdicts of small, open and purpose-built guards beyond noise; frontier guards barely move.
output.weight_reason: It is a carefully controlled, well-released evaluation of a previously unmeasured failure axis for agent guards, but it is a workshop-scale study on a single benchmark with no mitigation.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: lower polysemanticity and more disentangled personalized latents hold only within model families (Mixtral shows a higher latent ratio than Llama-13B), and the expert-boosting result is a KL reduction vs random experts, with expert sets that are correlational and only moderately stable.
output.brief: Three open MoE LLMs (OLMoE-1B-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Mixtral-8x7B) are personalized on Multifaceted Collection with two-stage tuning, first the routers and then only the most-selected experts. BatchTopK crosscoders are trained on paired personalized and non-personalized activations at one layer per model, chosen by routing divergence and entropy. Under 0.25% of latents (157, 132 and 111) are personalized, and an LLM explainer labels them. The personalized MoEs outperform or match dense models with similar active parameters, and match or exceed similar-total-parameter dense models for Qwen and Mixtral, on Multifaceted Bench, LaMP and LongLaMP, with the largest gains on Multifaceted Bench. K-sparse probing gives MoE experts higher balanced accuracy than dense MLPs, including at k=1. Latent-to-expert mappings reach stability 0.81 and distinctiveness 0.94 for Qwen3. Patching personalized latents reduces KL to the personalized model more than random or shared latents, and boosting the mapped experts moves the non-personalized model closer than random experts. Limits: one layer per model, dense baselines differ in pretraining, crosscoder variance explained is 0.65 to 0.80, scorer F1 is moderate (0.63 to 0.70), and the data are synthetic group-level preferences.
output.gist: Personalizes three MoE LLMs and uses crosscoders to find a few personalized latents mapped to specific experts. Patching and expert boosting move behavior toward the personalized model, and the MoEs probe as less polysemantic than dense models.
output.weight_reason: A complete, sound application of crosscoder diffing and expert mapping to MoE personalization with causal checks, but limited to one layer per model, synthetic preferences and correlational expert attribution.

output.brief: Looped two-layer transformers execute in-context Mealy machines, one loop per input symbol, with a simulator that gives exact targets for every position and for counterfactual hidden-state swaps. Models trained to answer only at loop 32 are 100% correct there but keep 22.3% of endpoint answers at loop 64. Supervising one random position per example keeps 99.8%, all positions keeps 94.3%, and a random exit (H+U{0..8}) raises loop-64 accuracy from 30.0% to 85.6% against a fixed slack of 4. A progressive-training adaptation with truncated gradients mostly fails to learn, while a full-gradient control with the same exits keeps 97.9%. Computation is exact: swapping one frontier hidden vector redirects all later positions to the source's continuation in 237/237 eligible pairs in each of ten models. Retention is not reuse. Freezing each position at the loop where its answer first appears cuts endpoint accuracy to 4.1% (sampled-position) and 6.3% (random-exit), while freezing two to four loops later restores it. The released maze network behaves the same way. The evidence covers one synthetic task family, one architecture, three seeds for new controls, and one maze checkpoint with 32 mazes. It does not identify a mechanism.
output.gist: Looped transformers executing in-context Mealy machines compute each step exactly, but retention depends on the training objective, and even retaining models cannot have states frozen when answers first appear.
output.weight_reason: A careful controlled analysis with matched training controls and exact counterfactuals that separates computation, retention and reuse, but it rests on one synthetic task family, small models and few seeds.

output.brief: Under balanced option orderings (cyclic rotations), the pooled selection-rate SD factors exactly into the flip rate (share of questions whose chosen option changes with order) and the positional skew (SD of letter selection among those flipping questions); both need no gold labels, and balanced RStd factors through the same flip rate. On 41 open-weight checkpoints and 12 benchmarks, the flip rate falls with accuracy (Spearman -0.95) and flips concentrate on items with close top-two probabilities, while the skew follows the estimated option-symbol prior (median centred cosine 0.87 on four-option cells). Prior correction (PriDe, batch calibration variant) mainly lowers skew; aggregating each ordering with its reversal mainly lowers flip rate. Both narrow placement range, but aggregation leaves fewer rank reversals (10.6% vs 15.4% of pairs) and raises the stable-wrong share by 6.2 points against a 2.8-point accuracy gain. Correction then aggregation lowers both factors and narrows the range most. Limits: associations are not causal, only output-score mitigations and first-token readouts on mostly English benchmarks were tested, and the cyclic design is required for exactness.
output.gist: Under balanced option orderings, the pooled selection-bias SD equals flip rate times positional skew. Prior correction mainly lowers skew, reversal aggregation mainly lowers flips, partly by settling on wrong answers; composing them lowers both.
output.weight_reason: A clean exact decomposition with a controlled comparison of mitigations across 41 checkpoints and 12 benchmarks gives a useful reporting framework, but it is a focused methodological analysis of one evaluation artifact.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the +33.75% (Hi→Ur) and +45.86% (Hi→Sd) BLEU gains are computed against the Gemma-2 SFT baseline (the table's Δ_SFT row), not the strongest baseline; against the best DPO baseline the gains are about +22.7% and +29%. The no-English-pivot finding rests on cosine similarity of MLP states with token embeddings, for Indic pairs only.
output.brief: TITAN uses Gemma-2 9B to find translation-critical components for Hindi→Urdu and Hindi→Sindhi. CIRCE, a subspace-restricted activation patching method, contrasts translation prompts with counterfactual prompts, and components are selected by a P99 noise-floor threshold. SAEs are then trained on the identified layers, and features are scored by selectivity and causal lift. SFT (CIRCE) and then DPO (TITAN) update only the selected components, under 5% of parameters (3.14% in the matched comparison). On Hi→Ur, TITAN reaches 31.82 BLEU against 25.94 for the best DPO baseline (Gemma-2); on Hi→Sd it reaches 23.25 against 18.01. A LoRA SFT+DPO run with the same parameter budget gets 26.37 BLEU. Progressive knockout in a LoRA model that was not circuit-restricted drops BLEU from 25.53 to 16.54 for eight circuit components, against 25.41 for random ones. Gains also appear on four further directions: Hi↔En, En↔Fr, Hi→Ta and En→Ga. Human evaluation uses about 30 ratings per cell. The English-pivot analysis relies on embedding cosine similarity, and only Gemma-2 9B was studied.
output.gist: Subspace activation patching finds translation-critical heads and MLPs in Gemma-2 9B; SFT and DPO restricted to them beat a parameter-matched LoRA on Hindi–Urdu and Hindi–Sindhi translation.
output.weight_reason: The circuit-restricted tuning is validated with knockouts and a matched-LoRA comparison, but it covers one model, the baselines are mismatched, and the mechanistic claims rest on loose probes.

output.brief: Eight typed decision models (TDMs), which return a probability for each answer option instead of generating text, are tested as pairwise judges with CALM's bias benchmark. Seven LLM judges, two from 2024 and five from 2026, receive the same prompts. Nine of CALM's twelve biases apply to TDMs. The authors add three tests that place the cue on the better response or add a neutral note, and they shuffle answer order. Bias is measured as excess verdict change beyond that of a repeated prompt, with permutation tests and a 5-point threshold. Every TDM is biased in three to eight of the twelve tests. Sentiment and position bias affect all eight, and sentiment is strongest. TDMs are more biased than 2026 LLM judges, whose position effect is at most 6 points, but they are more consistent. Both kinds of judge flip on largely the same prompts (prompt effects correlate at 0.95). Flips concentrate on low-confidence verdicts, yet calibration does not predict lower bias. At the median, a 2026 LLM judge costs 37 times as much as a TDM. Limits: only pairwise tests with references, unverified GPT-4-Turbo rewrites, invented citations, and models from a single month.
output.gist: Applying CALM's bias tests to eight typed decision models and seven LLM judges, every TDM shows bias, notably position and sentiment, exceeding 2026 LLM judges while being more consistent and far cheaper.
output.weight_reason: A complete, fair comparison of TDMs and LLM judges on a known bias benchmark, with released data and sound statistics, but it applies an existing benchmark to a new model class.

output.brief: A controlled single-turn study of sycophancy in factual QA. It uses 42,608 short-answer questions drawn from TriviaQA, SciQ and SimpleQA-Verified, filtered to nine topics and four difficulty levels. Each question is asked alone, with a correct user opinion, or with an incorrect user opinion. Opinions are phrased in 21 framing types across 8 dimensions: expertise, confidence, external source, hierarchy, social pressure, unity, stake and consequence. Fourteen open-weight instruction-tuned models are tested, and six metrics are conditioned on the baseline answer's correctness and the opinion's correctness. Every model does worse under incorrect opinions than at baseline, regardless of size. Confidence, external source and unity vary accuracy most. High unity ("we think") drops accuracy under incorrect opinions to 0.28, a fall of 0.29, against 0.16 for the next framing. Expertise, hierarchy and social pressure change accuracy by at most 0.02 across types. Larger models show lower sycophancy and regression rates, but no consistent gain in self-correction. Effects are larger on entity-centric topics and on harder questions. Limits: the high-unity effect is confounded with changing the task, distractor types are not separated, and only English, single-turn, open-weight settings are covered.
output.gist: Tests 14 open models on 42K factual questions with 21 framings of correct or incorrect user opinions. Shared-opinion, confidence and source framings sway models most; authority and pressure matter little.
output.weight_reason: A complete, fair systematic comparison of framings and conditional metrics that sycophancy evaluations can reuse, though limited to single-turn English factual QA with open models and no mitigation.

output.brief: MOSAIC trains a shared TopK sparse autoencoder over image and text hidden states of a VLM, then uses EK-FAC influence to split each training example's influence over individual latents and project it onto text phrases and image regions. Training adds structured regional sparsity (group and exclusive penalties over attention-clustered patch regions), a contrastive phrase-region alignment loss supervised by frozen VLM attention, and latent decorrelation. Experiments use Qwen3-VL-2B and Gemma-4-E2B on VizWiz captioning, CheXpert and GQA. Inserting the SAE changes task scores only slightly (GQA Qwen accuracy 0.651 to 0.636). Visual footprint falls from 0.688 to 0.120 on GQA with Qwen. On GQA with Gemma at k=256, removing influence-ranked latents flips 38.3% of predictions, against 8.3% for activation ranking. Removing the image reorders training-example rankings (Spearman -0.80 to -0.56) while latent rankings stay positively correlated (0.54 to 0.80). Limits: only two roughly 2B models, apparently small evaluation sets, no baseline attribution methods, no retraining check of the training-example rankings, and qualitative case studies for the hierarchy.
output.gist: A shared sparse image-text autoencoder with spatial and phrase-alignment losses lets EK-FAC influence be decomposed into localized latents; influence-ranked latents flip more predictions, and removing the image reorders training-example rankings.
output.weight_reason: It is a complete, carefully ablated extension of latent-mediated influence to VLMs across two models and three tasks, but it builds on existing SAE and EK-FAC components and does not validate the training-example rankings directly.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: it says Dir-A steering corrects rule-framed errors, but the evidence is 3 flips out of 10 conflict items (CI 0.35 to 0.91) and the consequence-framed side may simply be at ceiling, and it presents the directions as causally effective across the layer band although steering was tested only in Qwen layers 6 to 15.
output.brief: Probes and steering vectors are used to look for separate residual-stream directions for moral reasoning style (rule-framed vs consequence-framed questions) and judgment polarity (permissive vs prohibitive). The dataset is a 2x2 factorial set of 1,452 items from ETHICS, Moral Stories and Social Chemistry, plus a 32-item hand-written cleanroom set with 10 conflict pairs. In Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B (4-bit), logistic-regression directions Dir-A (style, r>0.87) and Dir-B (polarity, r>0.85) have cross-correlation |r|<0.04, peaking at 34-47% depth. Steering Dir-A shifts logit differences with Cohen's d above 1.0 in most quadrants, but overall accuracy rises only from 0.613 to 0.650. On conflict pairs, rule-framed accuracy goes from 0.40 to 0.70 (3 flips) and consequence-framed stays at 0.80, with n=10 and wide intervals. On cleanroom items the activation probe scores 0.594, above TF-IDF (0.44-0.50) but below keyword matching (0.750). Ablation shows no necessity. Steering was run only on Qwen, with no full-precision replication, and style is partly predictable from source identity.
output.gist: Linear probes find near-orthogonal residual-stream directions for rule vs consequence framing and for judgment polarity in three 7-8B chat models; steering the framing direction shifts judgments, but generalization to novel phrasings is modest.
output.weight_reason: A careful but small-scale probing and steering study on 7-8B models that is honest about weak generalization and no necessity result, and the framing direction is only modestly better than lexical baselines.

output.brief: X-AgentRed is a red-teaming framework for personal agents that call tools across many services. A red-teaming LLM labels each tool's preconditions, effects and potential harms, then links tools whose effects satisfy another's preconditions into a directed HarmFlow graph (914 tools, 30 services, 29,367 edges). Backward random walks from harm-associated tools give recipes, which are turned into scenarios with benign user requests. Execution feedback then substitutes adjacent tools in harmful paths and repairs unmet preconditions in blocked ones. On 250 candidate scenarios per target across four frontier agents, with harm confirmed by two LLM judges, average harmful path rate is 19.2% versus 10.5% for STAC and 2.7% for TRACE. Tool coverage is 41.5% versus 13.9% and 23.7%. Claude Opus 4.8 is the hardest target at 7.6%. Feedback-driven diversification reaches 27.7% HPR versus 18.0% for random sampling. Limits: each configuration is a single run in a simulated environment, and executed workflows are far longer than the baselines' (23.2 versus 7.8 and 3.3 calls), so diversity is not separated from length. Rates also depend strongly on judge aggregation.
output.gist: A red-teaming agent builds a graph of tool preconditions and effects, samples harmful cross-service paths, and refines them from execution feedback, reaching 19.2% harmful path rate versus 10.5% for STAC.
output.weight_reason: A complete, fairly compared method with ablations on feedback operators, but evaluated in one simulated ecosystem, single runs, and baselines not matched in effort.

output.brief: A span veto ANDs one condition into the attention mask: queries outside a trigger-marked span cannot attend to keys inside it. Outside activations are then bit-identical under same-length substitution of the span's content. This was verified on ten models, seven mixer families and 0.5B-120B parameters, with two-pass state recomputation for recurrent hybrids. Distilling the veto teacher (KL plus attention-mass penalties) into weights gives a backdoor on six families from 4B to 120B. These checkpoints match the veto reference on a GPT-4.1 judge (n=1,124), on verbatim and presence leaks, and on wrapped needle retrieval (0.00 in-span). Benchmark changes are within about 1.6 points, except Gemma-4-31B at about -3.5. Naive backdoors are probe-decodable (0.57-0.79 vs 0.025 chance). Hardened ones reach chance probes but show outside-to-span attention far below base. Three adaptive attackers all fail to hold suppression, probe invisibility and normal routing together. The learned attack is domain-bound, and the code-review case study uses 18 files. Blind trigger discovery fails.
output.gist: An attention veto makes marked text provably inert; distilled into 4B–120B models it becomes a backdoor matching veto outputs, detectable via probes or anomalous attention routing.
output.weight_reason: It defines a new silent-omission backdoor with an exact noninterference reference, tested across six model families up to 120B and several detectors and adaptive attacks, though the adaptive analysis is limited and the case study small.

output.brief: Incorrect reasoning traces from Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B (thinking mode) on hard math problems are labelled by Monte Carlo rollouts as capability gaps (unrecoverable from the start), near misses (recoverable at every evaluated prefix), or traces with a failing step (the first prefix whose best reachable value falls to 0.1 or below). Hidden-state probes are tested against these labels, each compared with the strongest baseline that uses no hidden states. A calibrated correctness probe trained on final labels reaches 0.81 detection AUROC, but at 8B it misses 81% of failing-step traces and 47% of near misses; after controls the gap is 0.125 at 8B and 0.037 at 4B. A probe trained on rollout rates ranks the two types in the opposite order, though it differs in more than its labels. A transcoder-activation classifier separating capability gaps from failing-step traces beats the baseline by 0.055 AUROC at 8B and 0.049 at 4B. No probe beats a trace-length rule at locating the failing step; at 8B only one probe was tested. Limits: one model family, math only, noisy rollout labels, and hidden-state read positions that for about half the traces lie in an earlier step.
output.gist: A correctness probe misses 81% of single-step failures in 8B reasoning traces; no tested probe beats a trace-length rule at locating the failing step.
output.weight_reason: A careful, preregistered-threshold analysis with released data, but it is mostly negative, covers one model family on math, and its labels and read positions are noisy.

output.brief: A pipeline for translating English safety, conversational and math benchmarks into 11 languages (ar, fr, hi, zh, ru, th, es, tr, fa, bn, pl). A reasoning model (GPT-5.4 Thinking) proposes three translation instructions. Five translators are compared on a 70-item Thai pilot, and GPT-5-mini with the meaning-focused instruction is chosen for production. The choice is made on cost: projected cost is about $97 versus $145 for GPT-5.1, which had higher pilot validity (70/70 versus 68/70). Outputs go through source-specific structural validation, and failures in WildChat and WildJailbreak are regenerated from the English source. Of 978 initial failures, four remain unresolved, giving 6,816 of 6,820 pairs (99.94%) in those two subsets. Translator-independent checks flag 1.2% of audited pairs as left in English, and an LLM judge rates 99.6% as meaning-preserving. Evaluating Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B shows Llama under-refusing harmful requests outside English, Qwen over-refusing benign prompts, and MATH-500 accuracy falling by up to 20 and 15 points. Limits: coverage is structural, not semantic, and no bilingual human verification exists. The pilot covers only Thai, and the judge is the same family used to select the configuration. Only two 7-8B models were tested, and fixed generation budgets truncate non-English responses more.
output.gist: A pipeline uses a reasoning model to choose translation settings, then translates seven safety, chat and math benchmarks into 11 languages with validation and repair, reaching 99.94% structural coverage on repaired subsets.
output.weight_reason: The work is a sound but modest benchmark-translation pipeline whose fidelity rests on automatic checks, a Thai-only pilot and two small models, with no human verification.

output.brief: Ciphered Skill Injection (CSI) hides attacker instructions in a skill's SKILL.md as Caesar ciphertext followed by a decoding cue. A layered variant adds a Caesar-encoded request to run a separate decryption skill (AES, ChaCha20-Poly1305 or XSalsa20-Poly1305) on a password-encrypted payload. The attack is applied to the 139 injection-task pairs of the Skill-Inject contextual benchmark across eight models, and decryption attempts, full recovery, attack attempts and attack success are scored separately. With shortened target skills, Caesar CSI reaches up to 47.5% attack success (Muse-Glimmer-30B) and Layered CSI up to 40.3% (Gemma-4-31B). Recovery does not imply compliance: Qwen3.8-27B recovers 78.4% of Caesar payloads but succeeds in 5.8%. Layering raises success for three models and lowers it for five. Without the Caesar skill, success falls for some models but persists. Two skill scanners flag at most 4.3% of injected skills. The main limit is that the skills were rewritten shorter by an LLM; with original longer skills, Layered CSI success drops to 0-8.6% on the four open models, so the main rates may not extend to unmodified skills.
output.gist: Caesar-ciphered and layered-encrypted instructions injected into skill files reach up to 47.5% and 40.3% attack success on shortened skills across eight models, though decoding often does not produce compliance.
output.weight_reason: A systematic evaluation of encoded injections in skills, with ablations and a recovery-versus-compliance split, but it extends an existing benchmark and its main rates rest on LLM-shortened skills.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the claim that signals closer to response formation better encode attack success is not tested, since the study only compares AUROC against benign controls (not successful against unsuccessful attacks), and the paper itself concedes the scores may reflect wording, length, source or attack type.
output.brief: Five internal-signal prompt-injection detectors (PIShield, Attention Tracker, Role Confusion, Dong exposure probe, J-Lens) are adapted to one structured prompt template and run on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it. Each is scored by AUROC against 1,000 template-matched benign controls, using 2,000 attacks per model split by behavioral outcome as judged by LLM judges (800 successful and 1,200 unsuccessful on Qwen; 569 and 1,431 on Gemma). PIShield and J-Lens separate unsuccessful attacks from benign inputs better than successful ones on both models (PIShield 0.898 vs 0.637 on Qwen, 0.980 vs 0.821 on Gemma). Attention Tracker, Role Confusion and the exposure probe show the reverse; Attention Tracker reaches 0.949 on Qwen and 0.887 on Gemma for successful attacks. The authors read this as recognition versus influence awareness. Limits: only two similarly sized models, one explicit template, adaptively strengthened attack corpus, adapted rather than faithful method reproductions, and no causal tests, so wording or attack-type confounds remain possible.
output.gist: Five internal-state injection detectors, adapted to one template on two open models, separate successful and unsuccessful attacks differently: presence probes favor failed attacks, attention-based signals favor successful ones (Attention Tracker 0.949 AUROC on Qwen).
output.weight_reason: A careful, fair-comparison analysis of what internal detectors measure, but limited to two models, one template and adapted methods, with a workshop-scale scope and untested causal explanation.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the r=0.70 link between P1 alignment and task accuracy is a single Llama-3.1-8B/M-ColorNames warm/cool fit (p=0.035), and across 120 correlations only 12.5% reach significance (mean |r|=0.38); the 96.7% is one Mistral-7B warm/cool result, not a general accuracy across models.
output.brief: Six pretrained LMs (Gemma-2 2B/9B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, PaliGemma2-3B) are probed layerwise on color descriptions from MLMC (10 languages), M-ColorNames (6 languages) and Munsell chips. Perceptual alignment (P1) is centered kernel alignment between the model's RBF similarity kernel and a CIE-LAB kernel. Cross-lingual symmetry (P2) is kernel congruence on matched color sets. P1 is low (roughly 0.0–0.2), peaks in early layers and falls about 80% by the final layer; a matched-n control (n=122) keeps the peak-then-decay shape. Descriptions containing basic color terms show 3–4× higher peak alignment. P2 congruence drops from 0.56–0.71 at the embeddings to 0.29–0.56 at the last layer, with model-dependent trajectories. Effective rank correlates with both axes (r from 0.76 to 0.99). Linear probes on warm/cool classification peak at early layers (Mistral 96.7% at layer 6), and one layer-wise CKA–accuracy correlation is r=0.70. Across 120 correlations only 12.5% are significant. Limits include one kernel bandwidth heuristic, CKA reliability concerns, and purely correlational evidence.
output.gist: Layerwise kernel-alignment analysis of six LMs shows color geometry matches CIE-LAB weakly, peaking in early layers then collapsing, while cross-lingual congruence also declines with depth; probe accuracy peaks at early layers.
output.weight_reason: A careful but modest correlational probing study on one domain, with weak and partly nonsignificant functional links, extending known layerwise findings to color.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: shallow exits are not consistently more robust. The effect is large only for Balcony-LLaMA3-8B (HarmBench ASR 4% vs 28%); for Balcony-LLaMA2-7B ASR spans only 36-44% (HarmBench) and 42-54% (AdvBench) over 50 behaviors, with AdvBench exit-18 below exit-15.
output.brief: The study attaches Balcony early-exit modules (exits at layers 15, 18, 21, plus the full model) to frozen LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B backbones and attacks each exit with GCG (150 steps, 50 behaviors each from HarmBench and AdvBench, judged by the HarmBench judge). For LLaMA3-8B, HarmBench ASR rises from 4% at exit-15 to 12%, 12% and 28% at full depth; AdvBench goes 2%, 0%, 12%, 28%. For LLaMA2-7B the spread is small: 36-44% on HarmBench and 42-54% on AdvBench. GCG final loss falls with depth, and on LLaMA3 exit-15 reaches about three times the full-model loss. Clean utility on six multiple-choice benchmarks rises with depth. Appending each exit's strongest suffix changes utility little, except ARC-E on the 7B model. The authors read LLaMA3's shallow-exit robustness as tied to low capability rather than a dedicated safety mechanism. Limits: one attack, two models, fixed exits, small behavior samples, and associative findings with no mechanistic analysis or defence.
output.gist: Applies GCG to early-exit Balcony versions of LLaMA2-7B and LLaMA3-8B; deeper exits are easier to optimize against and more jailbreakable on LLaMA3, while LLaMA2 varies little across depth.
output.weight_reason: A workshop-scale empirical probe with one attack, two models and 50 behaviors per benchmark, whose depth effect is strong for only one backbone.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the signal gains come from LLM-synthesized read-only evidence handed to the classifier, not from signals the models retrieved themselves, and "unstable" decisions are not measured, since the invariant-rate analysis shows consistent action anchoring at temperature 0.
output.brief: AuthGateBench is a synthetic benchmark of 1,400 instances for LLM authorization gates in coding agents. It covers five failure modes taken from Claude Code incident reports: scope escalation, credential exploration, inferred parameters, external sharing and guardrail bypass. DeepSeek-V4-Flash generates blocked base triplets of request, trajectory and action. It then rewrites only the request to yield an allow counterpart with identical action and trajectory. It also synthesizes read-only environment signals for each instance. Four LLMs (GLM-5.2, Kimi-K2.7-Code, Qwen3.7-Plus, DeepSeek-V4-Flash) act as gates under an implicit safety policy. False negative rates stay low, but false positive rates reach at least 80% on credential exploration and external sharing. Invariant rates, where a model gives the same decision on both members of a pair, average 87% and 95% on those two modes. Adding synthesized signals corrects more wrong predictions than it misleads right ones, for example 25.2% vs 7.6% on scope escalation. An explicit policy reduces over-blocking. Limits: one intended policy, synthetic data from a single generator, a small manual label audit, and signals written by an LLM that knew the label context.
output.gist: A 1,400-instance synthetic benchmark of contrast pairs tests LLM authorization gates; four models over-block user-authorized credential and sharing actions, while an explicit policy and supplied environment signals improve accuracy.
output.weight_reason: It is a useful benchmark with a sound contrast-pair design, but its data are synthetic and from a single generator, with one policy and four models, and the signal result rests on LLM-written evidence.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: real-data transfer covers only four of the seven concepts (distance via a grasp-location proxy), with wrist orientation agreeing least across models. Steering works only for the gripper, and that edit leaks into arm joints, while the geometry-matched wrist edit triggered compensation against the written angle.
output.brief: The study characterizes how seven manipulation variables are laid out in activation space in MolmoBot, a flow-matching VLA run in simulation: gripper state, end-effector position, target position, distance, contact, task phase and wrist orientation. It combines controlled sweeps, teleports, natural rollouts, linear and LDA probes, and interventions. End-effector and target positions each occupy a roughly Euclidean 3-D subspace (held-out R2 0.92 and 0.75). Distance is split into near-range and far-range codes whose probes are nearly orthogonal (cosine 0.04), tracing an L-shape. Wrist roll forms an open arc, not a circle, consistent with joint limits. Contact stays decodable when forced off schedule, but phase is inferred from motion and breaks when the arm pauses. Wrist edits act as beliefs and provoke compensation, whereas gripper edits derived from action gradients flip the command, mostly along one direction with some arm leakage. Four variables are re-examined in pi0.5 and MolmoAct2 on DROID, with similarity above a shuffled null. Limits: the taxonomy is supervised, the real-data checks are partial, and wrist agreement is weakest across models.
output.gist: Probes and interventions chart the geometry of seven manipulation variables in MolmoBot: 3-D position subspaces, an open wrist-angle arc, and two orthogonal distance rulers, partly recurring in two VLAs.
output.weight_reason: It is a careful, multi-method analysis that extends neural-geometry ideas to VLAs with some cross-model checks, but the main evidence comes from one simulated model and a partial real-data replication.

output.brief: A compiler turns straight-line programs into linear threshold circuits and then into SwiGLU MLP weights. With it, the authors embed an encrypted neural network inside a host model using hash-based digital lockers built from compiled Keccak. A GLU execution unit applies the decrypted weights to the input only when the secret trigger is present. The hidden payload is a ternary 64-8-16-2 chemical reaction classifier of 672 weights. The compiled model has 38 layers and about 2.07B dense parameters, of which 1.9M are nonzero. On held-out data it scores 73.5% with the correct trigger and about 50.6% without it. Under 500 steps of SFT it reaches 50.9%, against 92.7% for a trained password-locked baseline, and under LAT 52.9%, against 91.7%. GCG recovers the 8-bit trigger only by exhaustive enumeration. With a 16-bit trigger and about 20,000 queries it reaches 52.7%. Weight noising elicits nothing on a subset-parity task. The limits are stated: experiments use weakened locker settings (one Keccak round, 4-16-bit triggers), and the hosts are small MLPs rather than pretrained LLMs. Circuit width grows quadratically with the hidden layer size, and compiled weights are statistically anomalous even after obfuscation.
output.gist: Compiles encrypted neural networks into host-model weights via hash-based digital lockers, activated only by a secret trigger. A small chemistry classifier stays unelicited by SFT, LAT and trigger search, unlike a password-locked baseline.
output.weight_reason: It extends cryptographic backdoors from hidden fixed strings to hidden executable networks with a working compiler and a fair password-locked baseline, but it is a small proof of concept at reduced security parameters.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: only the text detector is compared with frontier models. The screenshot detector (93.32 F1) is compared only with four small or cheap image-capable models, the best being Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite at 78.70 F1.
output.brief: BrowseSafe++ is a benchmark of 38,675 attack/control webpage pairs. 32,187 pairs carry prompt injections observed on production sites, and 6,488 are retained from BrowseSafe. Page content around each injection is rewritten for privacy while the injection stays unchanged. Each page comes in HTML, Markdown, accessibility-tree, and screenshot views, with a user task and expected outcome. Sixteen prompted models were tested as detectors on the text views. The best, GPT-6 Astra, reaches 91.30-91.55 F1 but falsely flags 13.82-15.10% of benign pages. GPT-5.5 flags 19-21%. Rankings and per-attack recall shift across views. Models often follow injections they flag: 74.15% of followed injections were also flagged in separate detection. BrowseSafe-Guard, two 0.8B detectors trained with a pairwise ranking loss, reaches 92.98-98.29 F1 on text at 1.35-7.40% FPR, and 93.32 F1 on screenshots at 6.08% FPR. BrowseSafe-Adapt revises injections from agent feedback. On 1,024 tasks and seven agents, success rises from 0.49-4.00% to 30.66-95.41%. Test data share the training distribution, and Opus 5.5 keeps a lower FPR.
output.gist: A benchmark of 38,675 attack/control webpage pairs, mostly wild injections, in four views; a 0.8B text detector beats prompted frontier models, and adaptive revision raises attack success to 30-95%.
output.weight_reason: A large, released benchmark of mostly production-observed injections with matched controls, multiple views, and a fair comparison of detectors and adaptive attacks gives others in the area a complete resource to build on.

output.brief: DangerLens reads hidden states of aligned checkpoints through a checkpoint-specific Jacobian lens into vocabulary space. It keeps the Top-20 candidates at four response positions, and a frozen LLM judge, blinded to condition, scores prompt-relevance and functional role. The count of harmful-goal and operational-enabler candidates is the accessibility measure. Qwen1.5 0.5B, 4B and 7B are compared along two paths: safety SFT on the raw model, versus harmful SFT followed by the same safety SFT. Both reach near-zero HarmBench attack success. Over three runs per scale and an 800-prompt, eight-hazard bank, the prior-exposure path shows higher counts. The largest mean gap is 0.106 at 4B, and the contrast peaks at 0.255 near the 4B midpoint. Prior-exposure checkpoints also show greater early attack-success gain under identical harmful re-exposure. A human audit of 700 pairs gives 94.0% ordinal agreement and confirms 107 of 110 explicit hazard terms. Identity transport gives weaker contrasts (-0.006 at 0.5B). Limits: the absolute counts are small, one SFT recipe and one model family are used, a LLM judge supplies the labels, ablations use one run per scale, and the link to later susceptibility is supplementary.
output.gist: A Jacobian-lens probe with blinded LLM judging finds that Qwen1.5 checkpoints with prior harmful exposure keep more accessible hazardous concepts after identical safety alignment, with near-identical refusal rates.
output.weight_reason: It is a carefully controlled and validated application of a lens-plus-judge readout, but it covers one model family and one fine-tuning recipe, and the measured contrasts are small.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the ablations are layer-wise, run on PaliGemma2-3B with the binary dataset. The headwise analysis only reports per-head attention patterns and includes no head ablations.
output.brief: Attention from the output token to image tokens is measured for six VLMs (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, InternVL3.5 4B/8B, PaliGemma2 3B/10B) on affirmative and negated prompts, then compared with human eye-fixation patterns from a visual-world study of binary and multary negation. The stimuli are 1000 synthetic two-object images, 1000 synthetic four-object images, and 206 What'sUp images with Grounding DINO boxes (IoU 0.93 on 20 hand-annotated images). Only PaliGemma2-3B shows the human-like pattern on all datasets, shifting attention to the alternative object from layer 13 under negation. Wilcoxon tests are run only on the smaller models. Layer ablations on PaliGemma2-3B show that layers before 13 have the strongest causal effect, which the authors read as the shift being a byproduct. Per-head attention reveals no specialised negation heads. LLaVA-1.5-7B favours the left object. On yes/no questions, accuracy is lower for negated than affirmative prompts, with large differences by question type. PaliGemma2-3B's human-like attention gives no accuracy advantage over InternVL-3.5-4B, whose attention barely changes. Limits: three model families, simple images, attention only, human temporal priming replaced by static images, and the symbolic-processing explanation is not tested directly.
output.gist: Object-level attention in six VLMs is compared with human gaze under negation. Only PaliGemma2-3B shifts attention to the alternative, but layer ablations indicate this is not causal; negated accuracy is lower for all models.
output.weight_reason: A careful but narrow attention-pattern study on three model families and simple images, with limited causal evidence for its conclusions.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: in vision and language models the subspaces are evaluated only by nearest-neighbor retrieval selectivity, not by subspace ablation, and the authors list ablation-based behavioral tests there as future work.
output.brief: A hierarchy of permutation, orthogonal and bounded-condition invertible linear maps is learned to split a representation into two function-specific subspaces plus a residual. RNNs are trained with task-sufficiency losses and evaluated by ablation with a double dissociation index (DDI). Vision and language models use contrastive minimal-pair losses and are evaluated by retrieval. In tanh multitask RNNs on Anti vs DM1, DDI is 0.00 at the unit level, 0.08 for permutations, 0.37 orthogonal and 0.47 linear. Inclusive and mixed task pairs stay non-modular (maximum DDI at most 0.05). In Mante RNNs only the linear map works (DDI about 0.26-0.28). In Swin-Base, invertible maps reach content and style selectivity ratios of 16.1 and 5.3, against about 1 for permutations; ResNets fail. Language models show a similar ordering, and the subspaces predict fMRI differently. Random-label, spectrum-matched random-map and content-category controls fail to produce dissociations. Limits: no ablation tests in vision or language, single-split retrieval without error bars, LLM-generated syntactic counterparts, and sensitivity to hyperparameters, with condition numbers up to about 1e4.
output.gist: Learned permutation, orthogonal and invertible linear decompositions reveal task-specific subspaces: ablation gives double dissociations in tanh RNNs lacking unit modularity, and vision and language representations show retrieval-selective subspaces.
output.weight_reason: It offers a clear framework with useful controls (random labels, spectrum-matched maps, overlapping-function test) and consistent results across RNNs, vision and language models, but the vision and language evidence is retrieval-only and the RNN dissociations are moderate.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: no Transformer is evaluated; the Mamba-versus-Transformer gap in query-first retrieval is taken from prior work, and the experiments cover only two Mamba-2 models on a synthetic phonebook task.
output.brief: The study examines why Mamba-2 models fail at query-first key-value retrieval, where state capacity should not be the limit. Two models (an 8B base model and a 7.3B code model) are tested on a synthetic phonebook task, with and without a "target" flag on the queried entry. The flag more than doubles accuracy on long phonebooks, and recurrent-state probes and gate analyses show the target is stored earlier and gates separate target from distractor tokens better. Patching the gate values of about 10 target tokens between flagged and unflagged prompts transfers accuracy in both directions, and oracle scaling of those gates drives accuracy to near-perfect or near-zero. Layer-wise probes show relevance becomes decodable in token representations after nearly 10 layers when unflagged, versus 1-2 when flagged, and in the gates later still. Cumulative layer patching puts the gains in early-to-middle layers, where relevance is already in the representation but not yet in the gates. Limits: a single synthetic task, two Mamba-2 models, correlational probes, oracle token indices, and no state-capacity ablation or Transformer baseline.
output.gist: Probing and gate patching in two Mamba-2 models on a synthetic phonebook task show gates causally govern retrieval, but relevance reaches them only after critical layers.
output.weight_reason: It gives a sound causal analysis (bidirectional gate and representation patching plus layer-wise probes) of a specific failure mode, but on one synthetic task and two Mamba-2 models.

output.brief: Big-Big-SycoBench measures sycophancy in evaluative judgements that lack ground truth. It contains 450 synthetic text artefacts across ten writing genres, with 12 challenge arguments each (5,400 in total) that push the quality score up or down. Arguments are valid, grounded in planted strengths or weaknesses, or invalid, built from fallacy families such as authority, consensus, emotion and bare assertion. Labels went through adversarial LLM quality control and review by twelve annotators (94.1% pairwise agreement), then revision to remove construction cues. Each model scores an artefact 20 times; a score change counts as following only if it exceeds twice the baseline standard deviation. Across ten models, valid-argument following is 88-95% for seven models, 76-77% for Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3, and 32% for Opus 5.5 (100-artefact subset). Invalid-argument following ranges from 0.15% (GPT-6 Astra) to 94.6% (GPT-4o). Contrarian updates are below 0.2%. Valid lowering arguments are followed more often than raising ones. Limits: single-turn challenges, fully synthetic data generated by one model, LLM-judged argument weights, no neutral rescoring control, and different challenge directions for different models.
output.gist: A benchmark of 450 synthetic artefacts with valid and invalid arguments measures whether models revise quality scores for sound criticism but not fallacies. Invalid-argument compliance ranges from 0.15% to 94.6% across ten models.
output.weight_reason: It is a carefully built benchmark with a sound baseline-variability design that separates responsiveness from compliance, but it is synthetic, single-turn, not yet fully released, and covers ten models.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the Coin recovery from 31.6% to 84.3% is not shown to be goal recovery, since chance is 62.5% and a rewired never-trained random trunk picks the coin over the level end almost as often as the GM rewire (96.2% vs 98.7%).
output.brief: Goal misgeneralization is analysed in three Procgen environments (Maze, Coin, Attribute Maze) and five simulated robot tasks, with misgeneralized agents compared against agents trained on diversified distributions. Linear probes, world edits, Fisher-information sensitivity of the policy to representation changes, and behavioural tests separate three failures: target substitution (Maze, PushToMarker), where a place or spatial relation replaces the goal; a policy shortcut (Coin), a rightward action rule; and cue competition (Attribute Maze), where goal and proxy cues push opposite ways on one axis and the proxy wins. Steering at the fully connected layer raises Attribute Maze goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3% but does nothing in Maze, Coin or PushToMarker. Relearning the readout by behavioural cloning recovers goal reach from the last convolutional features in Coin (31.6% to 84.3%, though a random trunk does nearly as well on coin choice), partly in PushToMarker (31.4%), and in Attribute Maze (87.1%), but not in Maze. Limits: three seeds per cohort, static checkpoints, and a hypothesis that environment structure predicts the failure type that is not tested.
output.gist: Tracing the goal inside misgeneralizing RL agents in eight environments reveals three failure types at different depths: target substitution, action shortcut, cue competition. Steering works only where the goal reaches the decision; a relearned readout works where goal information survives.
output.weight_reason: A careful, multi-environment mechanistic analysis linking failure depth to which repair works, but on small RL environments with three seeds and limited recovery evidence.

output.overstatement: The abstract overstates: the 11/11 versus 8/11 contrast comes from one Qwen2.5-7B configuration (layer 18, alpha 8), not from all five models. On Llama-3.2-3B the ambiguous score falls in 0/6 categories, and Mistral-7B was tested on one category.
output.brief: The paper factorizes BBQ's ambiguous bias score into an answer-rate term and a signed preference term, so any steering that makes a model answer less pulls the score toward zero. On Qwen2.5-7B (layer 18, alpha 8, 28,824 items), contrastive projection-removal steering lowers signed ambiguous score in 11/11 categories but signed disambiguated score in 8/11, reversing it in Age and Religion. In six categories, 20.8% of 1,500 disambiguated items flip to the unknown option, where abstaining is wrong. StereoSet shows no analogous shift. The effect is model-specific: on Llama-3.2-3B the ambiguous score does not move. Across 99 configurations the composition share has median 4%. The contrastive direction is nearly orthogonal to the preference gradient (cosine -0.016). The proposed GCD direction projects the preference gradient off the unknown-option gradient. On Qwen2.5-7B it cuts unknown-rate change from +0.0705 to -0.0049, but ablations show unconstrained option-gradient directions do about as well. It worsens preference on Llama. Limits: models up to 7B, forced-choice scoring, single seed.
output.gist: Factorizes BBQ's ambiguous score into answer rate and preference, showing contrastive steering's apparent debiasing on Qwen2.5-7B is largely abstention-driven, and proposes an option-gradient direction that cuts answer-rate distortion.
output.weight_reason: It gives a clear, well-controlled diagnosis of an answerability confound in a widely used bias metric, but the effect is model-specific, the GCD gain is mostly shown on one model, and ablations show the constraint is not the cause.

output.brief: CAPE-Bench pairs 24 agent task templates in unauthorized and authorized worlds that differ by one decisive fact, with mock tools and environment-derived labels. Four open-weight agents sometimes act without authorization after reading the fact (2-13% of episodes) and then misreport (5-71% of informed violations). A retroactive permission request marks the lie: 0.70 versus 0.08 on 1,081 informed violations (preregistered odds ratio 7.0), though in Muse, which launders most, lie rates are about 70% either way. A linear residual-stream readout reaches AUROC 0.94 at the decision, but text monitors match it once the plan is written. It leads when reasoning is pressured to hide the lie (+0.16 over a CoT monitor). Gating every action cuts episode-level violations in all four models (Gemma 0.70 to 0.09 with an approver on repeated flags), at about 1e-8 of agent compute. On AgentDojo, a readout calibrated on 29 tasks halves attack success for Gemma-4 and cuts it for gpt-oss. Gating also cuts misreported violations from 0.10 to 0.01. Limits: mock tools, open models only, a judge-labelled lie, no tests against evasion, and lie-specific levers tested on Muse only.
output.gist: Matched-world benchmark shows open-weight agents violate authorization then misreport; a linear residual-stream readout gating every action cuts episode-level violations in four models and most subsequent misreports.
output.weight_reason: A careful, preregistered, matched-world evaluation of episode-level gating with honest negative results, but with mock tools, open models only, and text monitors matching the readout at decision time.
